extracted.intended_audience: Catholic clergy and preachers (especially those addressing university/academic audiences)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and delivering University sermons: selecting a suitable subject for an academic audience, preparing it with study and (usually) written composition, and delivering it with sincerity and adaptation to the hearers. Emphasises definiteness of object, intellectual instruction, and appropriate mode of treatment for the university context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnestness / inward conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: The preacher's eloquence must come from deep, genuine conviction and love; this interior earnestness naturally produces simplicity, gravity, emphasis, and peremptoriness in delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manifestation should be 'inflammata sint verba, non clamoribus gesticulationibusve immodicis' — words inflamed by the heart, not noisy gestures. Avoid artificial mannerisms; external manifestations should flow from internal intellectual and affective conviction (St. Francis de Sales, St. Augustine). Example anti-pattern: flashy gestures or declamatory affectation unbacked by real conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim at imparting a definite spiritual good
rubrics_metrics.description: A sermon must be directed toward conveying some definite spiritual benefit to hearers rather than producing a fortuitous or vague effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and study are necessary: choose a specific subject (fact, truth, doctrine, principle, or sentiment), master it, and make it the one business of the discourse. Avoid vague generalities about 'virtue' or 'Heaven' which fail to fix an impression. The preacher should seek to imprint something on the heart that will not leave it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness of object / single proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with a distinct categorical proposition that can be expressed in words and orient the whole sermon toward bringing out that one proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject any remark, however eloquent, that does not tend to bring out the chosen proposition. Avoid preaching on multiple subjects at once — even sequencing several topics in one sermon risks delivering several sermons without break. This is presented as the 'one virtue' of the preacher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address intellect as well as affections (teach and move)
rubrics_metrics.description: A preacher must not merely seek to move feelings but must instruct the intellect — 'Necesse est ut doceat et moveat' — convincing as well as persuading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: St. Ignatius: act of intellect should precede affections. Practical example: simple explanations of Mass attracted a congregation when oratory alone did not. Aim to inform and convince; mere sympathy/emotion alone will not fix conviction in hearers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and adapt to the hearer (audience analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how to preach only after perceiving the disposition of mind of those present — 'Debet prædicator perspicere, ne plus prædicet, quàm ab audiente capi possit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise particular ranks, professions, ages, educations of the university auditory. Rhetorical principle: persuasion requires knowing whom you address. Avoid preaching material beyond the audience's capacity and tailor examples and depth accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select subjects particularly suitable to a university audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose themes that speak to temptations of youth and intellect: sins against virtue and against faith (e.g., rash speculation, doubt, infidelity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: University-appropriate topics include improvement of time, avoiding occasions of sin, frequenting the Sacraments, inspirations of grace, consistency of the Catholic faith, philosophy of tradition, relation of Scripture to the Church, beauty of rites. Avoid treating full-length theological courses, polemical treatises, or panegyrics as 'sermons' (those belong to lectures/divinity school).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious when diagnosing the audience's moral condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Before addressing a presumed ethical deficiency of the hearers, be sure you understand their actual condition to avoid harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If mistaken about the audience you may do harm rather than good. When in doubt, prefer general safe topics rather than ambitious, targeted charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address sensitive or corrective topics covertly
rubrics_metrics.description: When tackling special dangers or deficiencies, treat them indirectly rather than ostentatiously announcing the theme (avoid blunt or commonplace reproaches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer particular topics that will 'penetrate and reach their mark' without explicitly proclaiming the main reason the sermon was chosen; avoid common-places and public reproach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of treatment: greater exactness and study for academic audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: University sermons should be treated with more careful study, a more accurate conception of the idea, cautious use of words, consultation of writers of authority, and somewhat more philosophical and theological knowledge than popular exhortations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This does not require ostentation of learning. The sermon should be unpretending; excessive display of erudition is unnecessary and may offend. Match depth of treatment to the audience without vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pretension and ornament for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not cultivate eloquence, learning, or style as ends in themselves; they must be subordinate to the evangelical object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lavish ornament, forced erudition, or originality that distracts from the single proposition. Eloquence is a gift but must not overshadow the end of preaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation: composition and writing as useful discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Study and writing are important preparatory acts for University sermons: writing stimulates clarity, logical arrangement, illustrations, and reveals gaps in knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal preparation (sketch, abstract, or full manuscript) is generally necessary for occasional or important university discourses. Parish priests with repetitive elementary topics may not need such formal composition, but for select occasions writing aids mastery and future preservation/publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript vs extempore delivery: prefer speaking without book when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: While preparation in writing is advisable, the act of delivery should be as near to preaching (personal, direct) as possible — preaching is not reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a manuscript is used, conceal it and avoid reading line-by-line; look up and address the audience. Memorising is presented as the most effective concealment. Reading a sermon as if reading a book risks reducing public worship to something replaceable by private reading and weakens the distinct value of public preaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of manuscript if used
rubrics_metrics.description: If a preacher brings a manuscript into the pulpit, he should conceal its use as much as practicable and not present the delivery as mere reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more a preacher looks off his manuscript and directly addresses the audience, the more he will be considered to preach. Conversely, slavish following of the manuscript indicates reading rather than preaching and diminishes effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal presence and individuality of the preacher
rubrics_metrics.description: Preaching draws people by who says it and how; the preacher's personal antecedents, voice, tones, and presence communicate something public printed words cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike sacramental ministers whose ritual action is standardized, the preacher resumes individuality and personal influence when delivering a sermon. The authenticity and freshness of the preacher's speech ('out of the abundance of the heart') are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly intricate argumentation unsuitable for oral delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not craft discourses so delicate or complicated that they require a book to be delivered or to be followed by hearers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a sermon needs a book for teaching, it also needs a book for learning; such fine, precise organizations of thought may be more appropriate for written treatises than oral sermons. Anti-pattern: constructing arguments that only work when read word-for-word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve records of important University sermons
rubrics_metrics.description: Because University sermons often receive more preparation and may be intended for broader defence or publication, keep sketches, abstracts, or full manuscripts for later preservation or press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even the least elaborate sketch is a useful record; minute and copious notes may later be adapted for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt style of treatment to different audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: The same subject may be treated differently according to hearers (example: St. Paul's different approaches to Jews, Areopagus philosophers, and general crowds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match examples, level of learning, and argumentative form to the audience's expectations and capacities; academic audiences permit more exact treatment but not gratuitous erudition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sermon-purpose from lecture/polemical composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Long theological courses, polemical treatises, panegyrics, or extended doctrinal expositions are better classed as lectures or scholastic works than as University sermons intended primarily for edification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve the pulpit for sermons proper (aimed at spiritual good of the hearers); use divinity-school formats for works intended mainly for defence of Catholicism at large or for publication as treatises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep scope appropriate to occasion (select a single point when necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: For large subjects, select one point or a single aspect to develop so the sermon remains focused and accessible given the limits of the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges the temptation to tackle too large a field; better to select and develop one illuminating point thoroughly than to attempt broad, superficial coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: On relations of Theology and Science: keep domains distinct and avoid forced conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: When addressing relations between Revelation and Physical Science, distinguish natural from supernatural knowledge and avoid presuming an essential conflict between physics and theology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the intersection carefully: some truths are both natural and supernatural, but largely the two fields are separate and incommunicable; avoid broad assertions of incompatibility. Practical rhetorical advice: choose a manageable point and clarify definitions when engaging scientific audiences.
